Nearly Sharp Bounds for Lattice Coverings by Convex Bodies

Heng Li ††thanks: School of Mathematics, Shandong University, Jinan, China, and Extremal Combinatorics and Probability Group, Institute for Basic Science, Daejeon, South Korea. Email:˜heng.li@sdu.edu.cn.    Xizhi Liu ††thanks: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China. Email:˜liuxizhi@ustc.edu.cn.
Abstract

For an nn-dimensional convex body KK, let θL​(K)\theta_{L}(K) denote its lattice covering density, and let ΘLconv​(n)\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n) and ΘLsym​(n)\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n) be the corresponding worst-case quantities over all convex bodies and over origin-symmetric convex bodies, respectively. Before this work, these quantities were known only to lie between a lower bound of order nn and an upper bound of order n2n^{2}, so even their polynomial order was undetermined. We prove that there are absolute constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that

c​n​log⁡n≤ΘLsym​(n)≤ΘLconv​(n)≤C​n​log⁡n​(log⁡log⁡n)10/3+o⁡(1).cn\log n\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.

Thus both worst-case quantities are n​log⁡n​(log⁡n)o⁡(1)n\log n\,(\log n)^{o(1)}, and the upper and lower bounds differ by a factor at most (log⁡log⁡n)10/3+o⁡(1)(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.

For the upper bound, a vertical–horizontal amplification based on weighted Boolean cubes combines covering estimates for low-codimensional sections into an exact lattice covering of an arbitrary convex body. For the lower bound, a random-slab construction and Poisson witnesses on flat tori show, with positive probability, that the resulting body admits no lattice covering of density below c​n​log⁡ncn\log n.

Keywords. Lattice covering; convex body; geometry of numbers; finite-field Kakeya; random slabs; Poisson process.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 11H31, 52C17, 52A23, 60D05.

1 Introduction

1.1 Lattice coverings and the extremal problem

A convex body in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. If v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n} is a basis of a full-rank lattice Λ⊆ℝn\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, write detΛ≔|det(v1,…,vn)|\det\Lambda\coloneqq|\det(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})| for its positive covolume. The translates {K+λ:λ∈Λ}\{K+\lambda\colon\lambda\in\Lambda\} form a lattice covering if

Λ+K≔⋃λ∈Λ(λ+K)=ℝn.\Lambda+K\coloneqq\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\lambda+K)=\mathbb{R}^{n}.

The density of this covering is voln⁡(K)/detΛ\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)/\det\Lambda. The lattice covering density of KK is

θL​(K)≔inf{voln⁡(K)detΛ:Λ+K=ℝn}.\theta_{L}(K)\coloneqq\inf\left\{\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)}{\det\Lambda}\colon\Lambda+K=\mathbb{R}^{n}\right\}.

This quantity is invariant under invertible affine transformations of KK.

We study the largest possible lattice covering density in a fixed dimension. Define

ΘLconv​(n)\displaystyle\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n) ≔sup{θL​(K):K⊆ℝn​ is a convex body},\displaystyle\coloneqq\sup\left\{\theta_{L}(K)\colon K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ is a convex body}\right\},
ΘLsym​(n)\displaystyle\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n) ≔sup{θL​(K):K⊆ℝn​ is an origin-symmetric convex body}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sup\left\{\theta_{L}(K)\colon K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ is an origin-symmetric convex body}\right\}.

The defining classes immediately give ΘLsym​(n)≤ΘLconv​(n)\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n).

All logarithms are natural unless a base is displayed, and all asymptotic statements involving nn are taken as n→∞n\to\infty. In the upper-bound construction, statements involving only the auxiliary dimension dd are taken as d→∞d\to\infty. For positive quantities aa and bb, write a≍ba\asymp b if a/ba/b is bounded above and below by positive absolute constants in the relevant limit, and write a≫ba\gg b if a/b→∞a/b\to\infty.

Rogers [29] gives a classical treatment of packing and covering. For the broader geometry of numbers, see Gruber and Lekkerkerker [16]; Conway and Sloane [4] give an extensive account of lattices and sphere packings.

1.2 Previous bounds

For comparison, Rogers [26] proved that arbitrary translates cover every nn-dimensional convex body with density n​log⁡n+n​log⁡log⁡n+O⁡(n)n\log n+n\log\log n+O(n), while Fejes Tóth [11] obtained essentially the same density using O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) cosets of one lattice. The restriction to a single lattice is substantially harder.

For Euclidean balls, Dumer [6] obtained the sharper translative bound (1/2+o⁡(1))​n​log⁡n(1/2+o(1))n\log n, and Bukh, Gao, Liu, Pikhurko, and Sun [2] attained this density with controlled covering multiplicity and identified a limitation of random periodic constructions.

For lattice coverings, Rogers [28] proved the universal estimate θL​(K)≤nlog2⁡log⁡n+O⁡(1)\theta_{L}(K)\leq n^{\log_{2}\log n+O(1)}. Ordentlich, Regev, and Weiss [23] established the first polynomial universal bound, θL​(K)≤C​n2\theta_{L}(K)\leq Cn^{2}. In subsequent work, the same authors [24] obtained uniform multiplicity estimates at polynomial covering density and studied random Construction-A lattices.

Near-linear upper bounds with polylogarithmic losses were already known for bodies with sufficiently many orthogonal symmetries through Gritzmann [15], and for locally anti-blocking bodies and polytopes with few vertices through Schymura, Wang, and Xue [32]. For Euclidean unit balls B2nB_{2}^{n}, Gao, Liu, Pikhurko, and Sun [13] proved

θL​(B2n)=O⁡(n​(log⁡n)βball),whereβball≔12​log2⁡(8​π​e3​3)=1.85837​….\theta_{L}(B_{2}^{n})=O\bigl(n(\log n)^{\beta_{\mathrm{ball}}}\bigr),\quad\text{where}\quad\beta_{\mathrm{ball}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(\frac{8\pi e}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)=1.85837\ldots.

In the opposite direction, Coxeter, Few, and Rogers [5] proved θL(B2n)≥(e−3/2+o(1))n\theta_{L}(B_{2}^{n})\geq(e^{-3/2}+o(1))n. Together with the universal estimate of Ordentlich, Regev, and Weiss [23], this gave the following bounds before the present work:

(e−3/2+o(1))n≤ΘLsym(n)≤ΘLconv(n)≤Cn2.(e^{-3/2}+o(1))n\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn^{2}.

These estimates left a multiplicative gap of order nn; in particular, even the polynomial order of the worst-case lattice covering density was unknown.

1.3 Main results

The results of this paper narrow this polynomial gap to an iterated-logarithmic factor and place both extremal quantities at the n​log⁡nn\log n scale in the following precise sense.

Theorem 1.1.

There exist absolute constants c,C>0c,C>0 and a nonnegative sequence εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0 such that, for all sufficiently large nn,

c​n​log⁡n≤ΘLsym​(n)≤ΘLconv​(n)≤C​n​log⁡n​(log⁡log⁡n)10/3+εn.cn\log n\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+\varepsilon_{n}}.

Theorem 1.1 follows from the following two independent results. The first gives a universal upper bound for every convex body.

Theorem 1.2.

There exist an absolute constant C>0C>0 and a nonnegative sequence εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0 such that, for all sufficiently large nn,

ΘLconv​(n)≤C​n​log⁡n​(log⁡log⁡n)10/3+εn.\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+\varepsilon_{n}}.
Remark.

The exponent 10/310/3 of log⁡log⁡n\log\log n in Theorem 1.2 can be reduced to 23​log2⁡(2​π​e)=2.72946​…\frac{2}{3}\log_{2}(2\pi e)=2.72946\ldots by the two-stage binary correction developed in our companion note [21]. Our main goal in the present paper is to identify the n​log⁡nn\log n scale up to an iterated-logarithmic factor, rather than to optimize the exponent of log⁡log⁡n\log\log n.

The second constructs origin-symmetric bodies with large lattice covering density.

Theorem 1.3.

There is an absolute constant c>0c>0 such that, for every sufficiently large integer nn, there is an origin-symmetric convex body Kn⊆ℝnK_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

θL​(Kn)≥c​n​log⁡n.\theta_{L}(K_{n})\geq cn\log n.

The witness KnK_{n} constructed in the proof of Theorem 1.3 is already in John position, with John ellipsoid B2nB_{2}^{n}.

Since (log⁡log⁡n)10/3+o⁡(1)=(log⁡n)o⁡(1)(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}=(\log n)^{o(1)}, Theorem 1.1 gives

ΘLsym​(n)=n​log⁡n​(log⁡n)o⁡(1)andΘLconv​(n)=n​log⁡n​(log⁡n)o⁡(1).\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)=n\log n\,(\log n)^{o(1)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)=n\log n\,(\log n)^{o(1)}.

Thus the worst-case lattice covering density is determined up to a factor (log⁡log⁡n)10/3+o⁡(1)(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}. The upper bound also confirms and strengthens the conjecture of Schymura, Wang, and Xue [32, Remark 1.4] that θL​(K)≤C​n​(log⁡n)1+log2⁡e\theta_{L}(K)\leq Cn(\log n)^{1+\log_{2}e} for every nn-dimensional convex body KK.

For Euclidean balls, the universal upper bound asymptotically improves the factor (log⁡n)βball(\log n)^{\beta_{\mathrm{ball}}} obtained by Gao, Liu, Pikhurko, and Sun [13] to log⁡n​(log⁡log⁡n)10/3+o⁡(1)\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.

1.4 Ideas behind the upper bound

Choose an auxiliary dimension dd much smaller than nn, write n=m+dn=m+d, and split ℝn=E⊕F\mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F with dimE=m\dim E=m and dimF=d\dim F=d. For y∈Fy\in F, let Ky≔{x∈E:x+y∈K}K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\} be the horizontal section of KK at height yy. The vertical space FF is used to find a useful family of such sections above every translate, and the horizontal space EE is used to cover them. The challenge is to do this when the sections have different volumes and then encode all vertical and horizontal shifts in a single lattice.

To find useful heights, we fold a narrow Gaussian into the unit cube. Each base point determines Gaussian weights on its Boolean vertices. The folding identity separates the total weight of the cube from the way this weight is divided among its vertices. Entropy estimates show that no single vertex receives too much weight and that vertices with very small weights can later be removed while retaining almost all of the total.

Good base points must be available above every vertical translate. We select a movable information layer on which the total weight and both entropy bounds are controlled, and divide the unit cube into a finite-field grid. The high-rank Kakeya theorem of Kopparty, Lev, Saraf, and Sudan [20] gives a linear subspace such that every grid cell can be shifted into this layer. Construction A lifts the subspace to a lattice in FF. Every vertical translate then contains a Boolean cube with total normalized Gaussian weight d−5/2+o(1)d^{-5/2+o(1)} and the required entropy bounds.

We next place KK in isotropic position. The pointwise marginal theorem of Eldan and Klartag [9] supplies a low-dimensional subspace FF on which the section volumes satisfy

volm⁡(Ky)=(1+o⁡(1))​voln⁡(K)​γd​(y)\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})=\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr)\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)\gamma_{d}(y)

throughout the relevant range. A finite discretization replaces these sections by finitely many slightly smaller convex bodies while retaining their individual volumes. The mean-hole estimates of Rogers [27] and Schmidt [30] provide one horizontal lattice that works for every retained section. Shannon entropy controls the total load lost in pruning, while min-entropy keeps every remaining section within the range of the mean-hole estimate.

Finally, simultaneous horizontal shifts multiply the remaining uncovered proportions, and a finite-index shear incorporates all shifts into one lattice in E⊕FE\oplus F. A total horizontal load of order n​log⁡nn\log n makes the uncovered proportion small enough for Rogers’ completion lemma [28], which turns the almost covering into an exact one. The vertical construction costs d5/2+o⁡(1)d^{5/2+o(1)}. The min-entropy requirement leads to

d=(log⁡log⁡n)4/3+o⁡(1),d=(\log\log n)^{4/3+o(1)},

so the vertical loss is (log⁡log⁡n)10/3+o⁡(1)(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.

1.5 Ideas behind the lower bound

The lower-bound construction intersects a Euclidean ball and a cube with a Poisson family of slabs. In the normalization used later, a=2a=2, b=a​e1/nb=ae^{1/n}, and

KΠ=b​B2n∩[−1,1]n∩⋂u∈Π{x∈ℝn:|⟨u,x⟩|≤1}.K_{\Pi}=bB_{2}^{n}\cap[-1,1]^{n}\cap\bigcap_{u\in\Pi}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|\leq 1\}.

The expected volume of this body is comparable to κn​an\kappa_{n}a^{n}, and a fixed positive proportion of the realizations have volume of this order. The Euclidean ball gives a uniform outer-radius cutoff, the random slabs create the obstructions to covering, and the cube places the construction directly in John position. Indeed, the inclusions B2n⊆KΠ⊆[−1,1]nB_{2}^{n}\subseteq K_{\Pi}\subseteq[-1,1]^{n}, together with the cube’s contact points, show that the John ellipsoid is exactly B2nB_{2}^{n}.

Fix a lattice Λ\Lambda and a target y∈ℝn/Λy\in\mathbb{R}^{n}/\Lambda. Choose a representative y~∈ℝn\widetilde{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Each residual vector y~−λ\widetilde{y}-\lambda, with λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, determines a spherical cap of slab normals that remove it. For the targets used in the proof, all relevant residuals lie in a thin shell. The target is uncovered when every corresponding cap is hit by the Poisson process, so the problem becomes one of constructing and controlling simultaneous Poisson witnesses.

The caps belonging to one target can be strongly dependent. We cluster nearby caps and place a measurable slot in the common intersection of each cluster. An injective choice of one Poisson point from every slot witnesses that the target is a hole. A hierarchical common-lens estimate controls the activity of these witnesses and their self-interactions.

A greedy packing on the flat torus supplies

T=exp⁡((1/2−o⁡(1))​n​log⁡n)T=\exp\bigl((1/2-o(1))n\log n\bigr)

targets whose residual directions are separated across different targets. The packing remains valid in the cusps of lattice space because the image of a Euclidean ball in a flat torus has Haar measure at most its Euclidean volume divided by detΛ\det\Lambda. A continuous Poisson version of Janson’s inequality then makes the covering probability superpolynomially small for each fixed lattice. Finally, every lattice that could cover the random body has bounded covering radius and therefore a short basis. A stable net over these basis matrices makes the estimate uniform over all lattices.

The same n​log⁡nn\log n scale emerges from different balances in the two proofs. In the upper-bound argument, exponential decay in the total horizontal load means that a sufficiently large constant multiple of n​log⁡nn\log n reaches the (nn+1)−1(n^{n}+1)^{-1} threshold required by Rogers’ completion lemma. In the lower-bound argument, the target supply above absorbs the self-interaction cost eO⁡(R)e^{O(R)} of the Poisson witnesses throughout R≤c​n​log⁡nR\leq cn\log n, where R≔κn​an/detΛR\coloneqq\kappa_{n}a^{n}/\det\Lambda. Excluding every lattice in this range forces any covering lattice to have determinant smaller than κn​an/(c​n​log⁡n)\kappa_{n}a^{n}/(cn\log n), which yields the lower bound.

The remaining gap between Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 is the iterated-logarithmic factor.

1.6 Organization

The proof has two technically independent parts. Part I proves the universal upper bound. In Section 2, we fix the notation and state the external results used in that argument. In Section 3, we develop the weighted full-cube construction. In Section 4, we transfer its weights to sections of an arbitrary convex body and perform the finite-index lifting. In Section 5, we combine these ingredients to prove Theorem 1.2.

Part II proves the worst-case lower bound. In Section 6, we collect the spherical-cap, flat-torus, and Poisson tools. In Section 7, we define the random body and prove its volume and normalization properties. In Section 8, we construct good separated targets for a fixed lattice. In Section 9, we develop the common-lens Poisson witness method and prove the fixed-lattice estimate. In Section 10, we pass from one lattice to all lattices. Finally, in Section 11, we prove Theorem 1.3 and complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Part I Universal upper bounds

2 Tools for the upper bound

This section fixes the quotient-torus notation and states the four principal external inputs used in the proof: the Rogers–Schmidt mean-hole estimate [27, 30], Rogers’ completion lemma [28], the pointwise Gaussian marginal theorem of Eldan and Klartag [9], and the high-rank finite-field Kakeya bound of Kopparty, Lev, Saraf, and Sudan [20].

For a positive integer NN, write [N]≔{1,…,N}[N]\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,N\}. For R>0R>0, let BRr≔{x∈ℝr:∥x∥2≤R}B_{R}^{r}\coloneqq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\colon\lVert x\rVert_{2}\leq R\}. If Λ⊆ℝr\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} is a full-rank lattice, let 𝕋Λ≔ℝr/Λ\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{r}/\Lambda be the quotient torus. Let μΛ\mu_{\Lambda} be the normalized Lebesgue measure on 𝕋Λ\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, equivalently its Haar probability measure. Thus μΛ\mu_{\Lambda} is the unique translation-invariant probability measure on 𝕋Λ\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}. Let πΛ:ℝr→𝕋Λ\pi_{\Lambda}\colon\mathbb{R}^{r}\to\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda} be the quotient map. For a Borel set J⊆ℝrJ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r}, define the uncovered proportion

ρ¯​(Λ+J)≔1−μΛ​(πΛ​(J)).\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+J)\coloneqq 1-\mu_{\Lambda}(\pi_{\Lambda}(J)).

A full-rank lattice L⊆ℝrL\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} is unimodular if detL=1\det L=1. Let ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} denote the space of unimodular lattices in ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r}, and let μr\mu_{r} be the normalized SLr⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{SL}_{r}(\mathbb{R})-invariant probability measure on ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r}, with the normalization used in Siegel’s mean-value theorem [33]. Set b0≔14​log⁡2716b_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{27}{16} and ηr≔b0​r−3​log⁡r\eta_{r}\coloneqq b_{0}r-3\log r.

Let GLr⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbb{R}) denote the group of invertible r×rr\times r real matrices, acting as linear maps on ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r}. If A∈GLr⁡(ℝ)A\in\operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbb{R}), then θL​(A⁡(K))=θL​(K)\theta_{L}(A(K))=\theta_{L}(K) and ρ¯​(A⁡(Λ)+A⁡(J))=ρ¯​(Λ+J)\bar{\rho}(A(\Lambda)+A(J))=\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+J). Translations of the body leave both quantities unchanged. We shall therefore use affine normalizations and determinant-one shears without further comment.

The following formulation of the mean-hole estimate is recorded by Ordentlich, Regev, and Weiss [23, Theorem 2.3]. It originates in Rogers’ mean-value argument [27]; see also Schmidt’s closely related estimates [30].

Theorem 2.1.

There exists an absolute constant cRS>0c_{\mathrm{RS}}>0 such that, for every sufficiently large rr and every Borel set J⊆ℝrJ\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} of volume V≤ηrV\leq\eta_{r},

|∫ℒrρ¯​(L+J)​d​μr​(L)−e−V|<cRS​e−ηr.\left|\int_{\mathcal{L}_{r}}\bar{\rho}(L+J)\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{r}(L)-e^{-V}\right|<c_{\mathrm{RS}}e^{-\eta_{r}}.

The theorem applies to arbitrary Borel sets and hence to all labels for sections of varying volume used later. More precisely, if the desired lattice determinant is DhD_{h}, scaling to determinant one replaces a set JJ by Dh−1/rJD_{h}^{-1/r}J, whose volume is volr⁡(J)/Dh\operatorname{vol}_{r}(J)/D_{h}. This normalized volume is the load used in the horizontal argument. The upper restriction V≤ηrV\leq\eta_{r} is the reason for controlling the largest load at a Boolean vertex by min-entropy.

The last step of the argument uses Rogers’ completion lemma [28, Lemma 4] to turn a lattice with sufficiently small uncovered proportion into an exact covering.

Lemma 2.2.

Let C⊆ℝrC\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} be a convex body and let Λ⊆ℝr\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} be a lattice. If ρ¯​(Λ+C)≤(rr+1)−1\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+C)\leq(r^{r}+1)^{-1}, then Λ+(1+1r)​C=ℝr\Lambda+\left(1+\frac{1}{r}\right)C=\mathbb{R}^{r}.

We next record the pointwise Gaussian marginal estimate of Eldan and Klartag [9, Theorem 1]. Its role is to compare, simultaneously at every point of a low-dimensional ball, the volume of a section of an isotropic convex body with the standard Gaussian density.

For y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, write γd(y)≔(2π)−d/2e−∥y∥22/2\gamma_{d}(y)\coloneqq(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\lVert y\rVert_{2}^{2}/2}. We use the pointwise, rather than merely distributional, form of the central limit theorem for low-dimensional marginals of log-concave measures. Write Gn,dG_{n,d} for the Grassmannian of dd-dimensional linear subspaces of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, equipped with its rotation-invariant probability measure.

For a random vector XX with log-concave density fXf_{X}, choose the upper-semicontinuous log-concave representative of fXf_{X}. If F∈Gn,dF\in G_{n,d}, E≔F⟂E\coloneqq F^{\perp}, and PFP_{F} denotes orthogonal projection onto FF, define the FF-marginal density of XX by

ρF​(y)≔∫EfX​(x+y)​𝑑x,for ​y∈F.\rho_{F}(y)\coloneqq\int_{E}f_{X}(x+y)\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\text{for }y\in F.

This is the marginal operator used by Eldan and Klartag. By Prékopa’s theorem, ρF\rho_{F} is log-concave and hence continuous on the interior of its support.

Theorem 2.3.

There exist universal constants C,c1,c2,c3,c4>0C,c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}>0 with the following property. Let XX be an isotropic random vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with a log-concave density, and let 1≤d≤nc11\leq d\leq n^{c_{1}} be an integer. Then there is a set ℰ⊆Gn,d\mathcal{E}\subseteq G_{n,d} of measure at least 1−C​e−nc21-Ce^{-n^{c_{2}}} such that, for every F∈ℰF\in\mathcal{E}, the density ρF\rho_{F} defined above satisfies

|ρF​(y)γd​(y)−1|≤C​n−c3\left|\frac{\rho_{F}(y)}{\gamma_{d}(y)}-1\right|\leq Cn^{-c_{3}} (2.1)

whenever y∈Fy\in F and ∥y∥2≤nc4\lVert y\rVert_{2}\leq n^{c_{4}}.

Suppose that XX is uniform on an isotropic convex body KK, and fix fX≔𝟏K/voln⁡(K)f_{X}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{K}/\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K). Let E≔F⟂E\coloneqq F^{\perp} and m≔n−dm\coloneqq n-d. For y∈Fy\in F, define the horizontal section Ky≔{x∈E:x+y∈K}K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\}. The defining integral now gives

ρF​(y)=volm⁡(Ky)voln⁡(K)\rho_{F}(y)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})}{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)}

for every y∈Fy\in F. On int⁡(PF​(K))\operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)), the Brunn–Minkowski inequality [31, Section 7.1] also shows directly that y↦volm⁡(Ky)1/my\mapsto\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})^{1/m} is continuous.

The topological support of the projected measure is exactly PF​(K)P_{F}(K). The inclusion of the support in PF​(K)P_{F}(K) follows from compactness. Conversely, every relative neighborhood of a point of PF​(K)P_{F}(K) meets int⁡(PF​(K))\operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)), where the section-volume function is positive, and therefore has positive projected measure. In particular, ρF\rho_{F} is positive and continuous on int⁡(PF​(K))\operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)). Thus, once FF is chosen as in Theorem 2.3, the theorem compares volm⁡(Ky)/voln⁡(K)\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})/\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K) with γd​(y)\gamma_{d}(y) at every y∈Fy\in F satisfying ∥y∥2≤nc4\lVert y\rVert_{2}\leq n^{c_{4}}. This pointwise conclusion, rather than merely a distributional approximation, is what the vertical construction requires.

The fourth principal input collected here is a high-rank finite-field Kakeya theorem.

The polynomial method for finite-field Kakeya sets began with Dvir’s rank-one theorem [7]. Dvir, Kopparty, Saraf, and Sudan [8] later developed the multiplicity method and several extensions. Here we use the rank-kk theorem of Kopparty, Lev, Saraf, and Sudan [20, Theorem 1], stated below in the form we need.

Let qq be a prime power, let 1≤k≤d−11\leq k\leq d-1, and let Grd,k⁡(𝔽q)\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) denote the set of kk-dimensional linear subspaces of 𝔽qd\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d}. A set A⊆𝔽qdA\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} is a Kakeya set of rank kk if, for every C∈Grd,k⁡(𝔽q)C\in\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}), the set AA contains a translate of CC.

Theorem 2.4.

If A⊆𝔽qdA\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} is a Kakeya set of rank kk, then

|A|≥(1+(q−1)​q−k)−d​qd.|A|\geq\left(1+(q-1)q^{-k}\right)^{-d}q^{d}.

The form needed in the vertical construction is the following direct contrapositive.

Corollary 2.5.

Define the rank-kk Kakeya threshold by

ϑd,q,k≔1−(1+(q−1)​q−k)−d.\vartheta_{d,q,k}\coloneqq 1-\left(1+(q-1)q^{-k}\right)^{-d}. (2.2)

If B⊆𝔽qdB\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} satisfies |B|/qd>ϑd,q,k|B|/q^{d}>\vartheta_{d,q,k}, then there exists C∈Grd,k⁡(𝔽q)C\in\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) such that B+C=𝔽qdB+C=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d}.

Proof.

Suppose instead that B+C≠𝔽qdB+C\neq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} for every C∈Grd,k⁡(𝔽q)C\in\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}). For each such CC, some affine coset of CC is disjoint from BB and hence is contained in A≔𝔽qd∖BA\coloneqq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d}\setminus B. Thus AA is a Kakeya set of rank kk. By Theorem 2.4, |A|≥(1+(q−1)​q−k)−d​qd|A|\geq\left(1+(q-1)q^{-k}\right)^{-d}q^{d}, contrary to the assumed lower bound on |B||B|. ∎

We shall also use the elementary estimate ϑd,q,k≤d⁡(q−1)​q−k\vartheta_{d,q,k}\leq d(q-1)q^{-k}, which follows from (1+x)−d≥1−d​x(1+x)^{-d}\geq 1-dx for x≥0x\geq 0. Consequently, whenever the matching construction produces a set BB with ϑd,q,k<|B|/qd≤3​ϑd,q,k\vartheta_{d,q,k}<|B|/q^{d}\leq 3\vartheta_{d,q,k}, the subspace in Corollary 2.5 has finite-field covering load |B|​|C|/qd=(|B|/qd)​qk≤3​d​(q−1)|B||C|/q^{d}=(|B|/q^{d})q^{k}\leq 3d(q-1). The layer-to-grid matching that produces such a set BB is proved in Proposition 3.6.

3 The weighted full-cube construction

We now construct the vertical lattice and its Boolean weights. No Boolean vertex is discarded at this stage. The folded Gaussian identity separates the total weight of the full cube from its distribution among the vertices. Min-entropy controls the largest vertex weight, while Shannon entropy later controls the total weight discarded when vertices with small weights are removed.

All constants in this section are absolute. Every o⁡(1)o(1) term is a deterministic function of dd alone. We let d→∞d\to\infty and put

τ≔12​log⁡d.\tau\coloneqq\frac{1}{2\log d}. (3.1)

3.2 A movable information layer

For a probability density φ\varphi, its differential entropy is h(φ)≔−∫φ(x)logφ(x)dxh(\varphi)\coloneqq-\int\varphi(x)\log\varphi(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x whenever this integral is finite. Set a⁡(t)≔−log⁡f⁡(t)a(t)\coloneqq-\log f(t), so that h⁡(f)=𝔼​a​(T)h(f)=\mathbb{E}a(T).

The Berry–Esseen theorem is a quantitative form of the central limit theorem: when the variance stays bounded away from zero and the third absolute moment is bounded, the distribution function of a normalized sum of dd independent copies differs from the standard normal distribution function by O(d−1/2)O(d^{-1/2}) [25, Chapter V]. We use this estimate to show that a fixed-width information interval has probability of order d−1/2d^{-1/2}, uniformly when its location is shifted by O⁡(log⁡d)O(\log d). The next lemma records the moment bounds needed for this application.

≤∥I−𝔼​I∥22+2​∥V−𝔼​V∥2​∥I−𝔼​I∥2=O⁡(s)+O⁡(s)=o⁡(1).\displaystyle\leq\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\lVert V-\mathbb{E}V\rVert_{2}\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{2}=O(s)+O(\sqrt{s})=o(1).

We next match the continuous layer, the grid size, and the discrete rank. The strict inequality required by Corollary 2.5 must also survive integer rounding.

Bertrand’s postulate states that, for every integer N≥2N\geq 2, there is a prime strictly between NN and 2​N2N. 3.4 Construction A and the scaled weighted construction

We lift the covering subspace CdC_{d} to a Euclidean lattice so that every torus point can be moved into a selected grid cell. The stability lemma then transfers the information-layer estimates from the chosen representative of that cell to the actual point.

For every b∈Bb\in B, choose a representative

tb∈𝒢⁡(r)∩𝒬b.t_{b}\in\mathcal{G}(r)\cap\mathcal{Q}_{b}. (3.35)

Let redQ:ℤd→𝔽Qd\operatorname{red}_{Q}\colon\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} be coordinatewise reduction modulo QQ. Define the unscaled Construction-A lattice by

Λ0≔1QredQ−1(Cd)={zQ:z∈ℤd,redQ(z)∈Cd}.\Lambda_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{Q}\operatorname{red}_{Q}^{-1}(C_{d})=\left\{\frac{z}{Q}\colon z\in\mathbb{Z}^{d},\ \operatorname{red}_{Q}(z)\in C_{d}\right\}.

Equivalently, if c^∈{0,…,Q−1}d\widehat{c}\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}^{d} denotes the standard integer representative of c∈Cdc\in C_{d}, then

Λ0=ℤd+{c^Q:c∈Cd}.\Lambda_{0}=\mathbb{Z}^{d}+\left\{\frac{\widehat{c}}{Q}\colon c\in C_{d}\right\}.

Changing the integer representative of cc only adds an element of ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}, so the lattice is independent of this choice. Since Λ0/ℤd≅Cd\Lambda_{0}/\mathbb{Z}^{d}\cong C_{d}, its covolume is

detΛ0=|Cd|−1=Q−k.\det\Lambda_{0}=|C_{d}|^{-1}=Q^{-k}. (3.36)

This is the usual Construction-A lift of a linear code, as used, for example, by Erez, Litsyn, and Zamir [10].

To pass from a selected point of a good grid cell to every point in that cell, we need the following stability estimate.

Lemma 3.7.

If t,t′∈[0,1]dt,t^{\prime}\in[0,1]^{d} and ∥t−t′∥∞≤Q−1\lVert t-t^{\prime}\rVert_{\infty}\leq Q^{-1}, then

|H⁡(Pt)−H⁡(Pt′)|+|H∞​(Pt)−H∞​(Pt′)|\displaystyle|H(P_{t})-H(P_{t^{\prime}})|+|H_{\infty}(P_{t})-H_{\infty}(P_{t^{\prime}})| ≤C​Δd,\displaystyle\leq C\Delta_{d}, (3.38)

where

The two Gaussian summands defining ff give |(log⁡f)′​(u)|≤τ−1|(\log f)^{\prime}(u)|\leq\tau^{-1} for 0<u<10<u<1, with the corresponding one-sided bounds at the endpoints. Thus the mean-value theorem proves (3.37).

In the logistic coordinate y=(t−1/2)/τy=(t-1/2)/\tau, the function h2​(ey/(1+ey))h_{2}(e^{y}/(1+e^{y})) has bounded derivative. The function log⁡(1+e−|y|)\log(1+e^{-|y|}) is not differentiable at zero, but its two one-sided derivatives are bounded in absolute value; hence it is globally Lipschitz. Applying these Lipschitz bounds coordinatewise proves (3.38). The estimate (3.39) follows from (3.1) and (3.24). ∎

Passing to standard-Gaussian coordinates scales Λ0\Lambda_{0} by τ−1/2\tau^{-1/2} and hence multiplies its covolume by τ−d/2\tau^{-d/2}. Define the scaled vertical lattice and the scaling map by

Λv≔τ−1/2Λ0,andΨd≔τ−1/2Idd.\Lambda_{v}\coloneqq\tau^{-1/2}\Lambda_{0},\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi_{d}\coloneqq\tau^{-1/2}\operatorname{Id}_{d}. (3.40)

The next proposition is the output of the vertical construction. It places a full Boolean pattern above every vertical translate and records its total Gaussian weight, largest normalized weight, and entropy.

Proposition 3.8.

For all sufficiently large dd, the lattice Λv\Lambda_{v} defined in (3.40) has the following property. For every y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, there are λy∈Λv\lambda_{y}\in\Lambda_{v} and t~y∈[0,1)d\widetilde{t}_{y}\in[0,1)^{d} such that

𝖶y\displaystyle\mathsf{W}_{y} =d−5/2+o(1),\displaystyle=d^{-5/2+o(1)}, (3.43)

−∑ε𝗐y,ε𝖶ylog𝗐y,ε𝖶y\displaystyle-\sum_{\varepsilon}\frac{\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}}{\mathsf{W}_{y}}\log\frac{\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}}{\mathsf{W}_{y}} ≤d​s+C​d​s​log⁡d+o⁡(log⁡d).\displaystyle\leq ds+C\sqrt{ds\log d}+o(\log d). (3.45)

4 Sections of varying volume and weighted lifting

The vertical construction assigns a different Gaussian weight to each Boolean vertex. Equalizing the corresponding horizontal sections would lose this information. In this section we retain the volume of each section, find one horizontal lattice for all loads in a prescribed window, amplify label-dependent hole bounds, and insert the resulting shifts into a finite-index shear. The determinant of the final lattice is the product of the horizontal determinant and that of the scaled vertical lattice.

4.1 Discretizing sections of varying volume

Let K⊆ℝnK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body. After an invertible affine transformation, assume that the uniform probability measure on KK is isotropic. Fix an integer d<nd<n, put m≔n−dm\coloneqq n-d, and let ℝn=E⊕F\mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F be an orthogonal decomposition, with dimE=m\dim E=m and dimF=d\dim F=d, supplied by Theorem 2.3. For y∈Fy\in F, write Ky≔{x∈E:x+y∈K}K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\}.

For the uniform measure on KK, the definition of ρF\rho_{F} gives ρF​(y)=volm⁡(Ky)/voln⁡(K)\rho_{F}(y)=\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})/\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K). For FF supplied by Theorem 2.3 and all sufficiently large nn, so that C​n−c3<1Cn^{-c_{3}}<1, the lower bound in (2.1) is positive at every point of the open ball {∥y∥2<nc4}\{\lVert y\rVert_{2}<n^{c_{4}}\}. Each such point therefore belongs to the support of the marginal, which is PF​(K)P_{F}(K). Thus the entire open ball is contained in PF​(K)P_{F}(K), and, because the ball is open, each of its points lies in int⁡(PF​(K))\operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)). Consequently, throughout this range,

volm⁡(Ky)=(1+O⁡(n−c3))​voln⁡(K)​γd​(y).\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})=\bigl(1+O(n^{-c_{3}})\bigr)\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)\gamma_{d}(y). (4.1)

The horizontal sections vary continuously with yy, but the later union bound requires a finite family. The next proposition replaces all sections in the relevant ball by at most (C​m2)d(Cm^{2})^{d} slightly smaller model sections while preserving their volumes up to a factor 1+O⁡(m−1)1+O(m^{-1}).

There is an absolute constant C>0C>0 with the following property. Let m≔n−dm\coloneqq n-d, suppose that m≥2m\geq 2 and d≤nc1d\leq n^{c_{1}}, and let R>0R>0 satisfy

2​d​R<nc4.2dR<n^{c_{4}}. (4.2)

Ja\displaystyle J_{a} ⊆K~y,\displaystyle\subseteq\widetilde{K}_{y}, (4.3)
(1−1m2)2​m​volm⁡(K~y)\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\right)^{2m}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y}) ≤volm⁡(Ja)≤volm⁡(K~y).\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})\leq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y}). (4.4)

volm⁡(Ja)=(1+O⁡(1m+n−c3))​voln⁡(K~)​γd​(y).\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})=\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{m}+n^{-c_{3}}\right)\right)\operatorname{vol}_{n}(\widetilde{K})\gamma_{d}(y). (4.5)

where the contraction is about the origin. By (4.6), 0∈K~ya0\in\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}}. For any convex set CC containing the origin, r​C⊆s​CrC\subseteq sC whenever 0≤r≤s0\leq r\leq s. Since 1−m−2≤1−σ1-m^{-2}\leq 1-\sigma, we therefore have Ja⊆(1−σ)​K~ya⊆K~yJ_{a}\subseteq(1-\sigma)\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}}\subseteq\widetilde{K}_{y}, which proves (4.3). The second inclusion gives

volm⁡(K~ya)≥(1−σ)m​volm⁡(K~y)≥(1−1m2)m​volm⁡(K~y).\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}})\geq(1-\sigma)^{m}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y})\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\right)^{m}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y}).

4.2 A common horizontal lattice and simultaneous shifts

The next lemma applies the Rogers–Schmidt estimate to all model sections at once. The sections may have different volumes; only their individual loads enter the union bound.

Lemma 4.2.

Let mm be sufficiently large, let Dh>0D_{h}>0, and let Ja⊆ℝmJ_{a}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}, a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, be finitely many compact sets of positive volume. Define the load of JaJ_{a} by ua≔volm⁡(Ja)/Dhu_{a}\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})/D_{h}, and suppose ua≤ηmu_{a}\leq\eta_{m} for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Let 0<c<10<c<1. If

(1+cRS)​∑a∈𝒜e−(1−c)​ua<1,(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}e^{-(1-c)u_{a}}<1, (4.8)

then there exists a lattice Λh⊆ℝm\Lambda_{h}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}, with detΛh=Dh\det\Lambda_{h}=D_{h}, such that

ρ¯​(Λh+Ja)≤e−c​uafor every ​a∈𝒜.\bar{\rho}(\Lambda_{h}+J_{a})\leq e^{-cu_{a}}\qquad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal{A}. (4.9)

In particular, if |𝒜|≤N|\mathcal{A}|\leq N and T≤ua≤ηmT\leq u_{a}\leq\eta_{m} for every a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, then the conclusion with c=1/2c=1/2 holds whenever

T≥2​log⁡(2​(1+cRS)​N).T\geq 2\log\bigl(2(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})N\bigr). (4.10)
Proof.

For a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, the rescaled set J~a≔Dh−1/mJa\widetilde{J}_{a}\coloneqq D_{h}^{-1/m}J_{a} has volume uau_{a}. For a Haar–Siegel random unimodular lattice LL, Theorem 2.1 and ua≤ηmu_{a}\leq\eta_{m} give

𝔼L​ρ¯​(L+J~a)≤e−ua+cRS​e−ηm≤(1+cRS)​e−ua.\mathbb{E}_{L}\bar{\rho}(L+\widetilde{J}_{a})\leq e^{-u_{a}}+c_{\mathrm{RS}}e^{-\eta_{m}}\leq(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})e^{-u_{a}}.

Markov’s inequality therefore gives

ℙL[ρ¯(L+J~a)>e−c​ua]≤(1+cRS)e−(1−c)​ua.\mathbb{P}_{L}\left[\bar{\rho}(L+\widetilde{J}_{a})>e^{-cu_{a}}\right]\leq(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})e^{-(1-c)u_{a}}.

Condition (4.8) and a union bound produce one LL for which none of these events occurs. Taking Λh≔Dh1/m​L\Lambda_{h}\coloneqq D_{h}^{1/m}L proves (4.9). Under (4.10), the left-hand side of (4.8), with c=1/2c=1/2, is at most 1/21/2. ∎

The next result chooses shifts that make all relevant labeled Boolean intersections small at the same time. It will be applied to the horizontal quotient torus.

Let 𝕋\mathbb{T} be a compact abelian group with Haar probability measure μ\mu. Let U1,…,UN⊆𝕋U_{1},\ldots,U_{N}\subseteq\mathbb{T} be measurable, and suppose μ⁡(Ua)≤δa≤1\mu(U_{a})\leq\delta_{a}\leq 1, where δa\delta_{a} may depend on aa.

For I⊆[d]I\subseteq[d], a labeled pattern consists of a nonempty set P⊆{0,1}IP\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I} and a label map ℓ:P→[N]\ell\colon P\to[N]. Given a labeled pattern and z1,…,zd∈𝕋z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathbb{T}, define

𝒰I,P,ℓ​(z)≔⋂ω∈P(Uℓ⁡(ω)−∑i∈Iωi​zi).\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)\coloneqq\bigcap_{\omega\in P}\left(U_{\ell(\omega)}-\sum_{i\in I}\omega_{i}z_{i}\right).

For j∈Ij\in I and e∈{0,1}e\in\{0,1\}, let ιj,e:{0,1}I∖{j}→{0,1}I\iota_{j,e}\colon\{0,1\}^{I\setminus\{j\}}\to\{0,1\}^{I} insert the coordinate ee in position jj, and define the ee-slice

Pj,e≔{ω′∈{0,1}I∖{j}:ιj,e​(ω′)∈P}.P_{j,e}\coloneqq\bigl\{\omega^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{I\setminus\{j\}}\colon\iota_{j,e}(\omega^{\prime})\in P\bigr\}.

When Pj,e≠∅P_{j,e}\neq\varnothing, its induced label map is

ℓj,e​(ω′)≔ℓ⁡(ιj,e​(ω′)),for ​ω′∈Pj,e.\ell_{j,e}(\omega^{\prime})\coloneqq\ell\bigl(\iota_{j,e}(\omega^{\prime})\bigr),\quad\text{for }\omega^{\prime}\in P_{j,e}.

Thus a slice retains the original labels of its surviving Boolean vertices. A family 𝒞\mathscr{C} of triples (I,P,ℓ)(I,P,\ell) is slice-closed if (I∖{j},Pj,e,ℓj,e)∈𝒞(I\setminus\{j\},P_{j,e},\ell_{j,e})\in\mathscr{C} whenever (I,P,ℓ)∈𝒞(I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C}, j∈Ij\in I, and Pj,e≠∅P_{j,e}\neq\varnothing. This closure condition is exactly what the coordinate-by-coordinate induction requires: after one Boolean coordinate is fixed, every nonempty slice remains among the patterns controlled at the preceding stage.

Theorem 4.3.

Let 𝒞\mathscr{C} be a finite slice-closed family of triples (I,P,ℓ)(I,P,\ell), allowing both the coordinate set II and the pattern PP to vary. If L≥2​|𝒞|L\geq 2|\mathscr{C}|, then there are shifts z1,…,zd∈𝕋z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathbb{T} such that, simultaneously for every (I,P,ℓ)∈𝒞(I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C},

μ⁡(𝒰I,P,ℓ​(z))≤L|P|−1​∏ω∈Pδℓ⁡(ω).\mu\bigl(\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)\bigr)\leq L^{|P|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}. (4.11)
Proof.

If one of the factors on the right of (4.11) is zero, then the intersection on the left is contained in a translate of a null set, so the desired inequality holds for every choice of shifts. We may therefore consider only triples for which all relevant factors are positive.

For 0≤q≤d0\leq q\leq d, let 𝒞≤q≔{(I,P,ℓ)∈𝒞:I⊆[q]}\mathscr{C}_{\leq q}\coloneqq\{(I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C}\colon I\subseteq[q]\}. We choose the shifts inductively so that (4.11) holds for every triple in 𝒞≤q\mathscr{C}_{\leq q}. For q=0q=0, every nonempty pattern is a singleton, and the assertion is exactly μ⁡(Ua)≤δa\mu(U_{a})\leq\delta_{a}.

Suppose that z1,…,zq−1z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-1} have been chosen for 𝒞≤q−1\mathscr{C}_{\leq q-1}. This property will not be affected by the choice of zqz_{q}, because none of the earlier intersections uses the qq-th coordinate.

Consider a triple (I,P,ℓ)∈𝒞≤q(I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C}_{\leq q} with q∈Iq\in I, and put I′≔I∖{q}I^{\prime}\coloneqq I\setminus\{q\}. By slice closure, each nonempty qq-slice belongs to 𝒞≤q−1\mathscr{C}_{\leq q-1}. If only the ee-slice is nonempty, then

𝒰I,P,ℓ​(z)=𝒰I′,Pq,e,ℓq,e​(z)−e​zq.\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)=\mathcal{U}_{I^{\prime},P_{q,e},\ell_{q,e}}(z)-ez_{q}.

The two sets have the same measure, |Pq,e|=|P||P_{q,e}|=|P|, and the induction hypothesis gives the required bound without any loss.

It remains to treat triples for which both slices are nonempty. For such a triple, set A≔𝒰I′,Pq,0,ℓq,0​(z)A\coloneqq\mathcal{U}_{I^{\prime},P_{q,0},\ell_{q,0}}(z) and B≔𝒰I′,Pq,1,ℓq,1​(z)B\coloneqq\mathcal{U}_{I^{\prime},P_{q,1},\ell_{q,1}}(z). Then

𝒰I,P,ℓ​(z)=A∩(B−zq).\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)=A\cap(B-z_{q}).

For Haar-uniform zqz_{q}, Fubini’s theorem and translation invariance give

𝔼zq​μ​(A∩(B−zq))=μ⁡(A)​μ​(B).\mathbb{E}_{z_{q}}\mu\bigl(A\cap(B-z_{q})\bigr)=\mu(A)\mu(B).

The induction hypothesis bounds the last product by

L|Pq,0|−1​L|Pq,1|−1​∏ω∈Pδℓ⁡(ω)=L|P|−2​∏ω∈Pδℓ⁡(ω).L^{|P_{q,0}|-1}L^{|P_{q,1}|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}=L^{|P|-2}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}.

Markov’s inequality shows that the target bound fails for this triple with probability at most 1/L1/L. At most |𝒞|≤L/2|\mathscr{C}|\leq L/2 triples in 𝒞≤q\mathscr{C}_{\leq q} have two nonempty qq-slices, so the union of their failure events has probability at most 1/21/2. We may therefore choose one zqz_{q} that works for all of them. This completes the induction. ∎

If 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a family of labeled patterns in {0,1}d\{0,1\}^{d}, regard each (P,ℓ)∈𝒜(P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A} as the triple ([d],P,ℓ)([d],P,\ell). Its slice closure, denoted by scl⁡(𝒜)\operatorname{scl}(\mathscr{A}), is the smallest slice-closed family containing these triples. The crude family containing every labeled nonempty subpattern on every surviving coordinate set has size at most

∑I⊆[d](N+1)2|I|≤2d​(N+1)2d.\sum_{I\subseteq[d]}(N+1)^{2^{|I|}}\leq 2^{d}(N+1)^{2^{d}}.

Consequently, with 𝒞≔scl⁡(𝒜)\mathscr{C}\coloneqq\operatorname{scl}(\mathscr{A}) and L≔2​|𝒞|L\coloneqq 2|\mathscr{C}|,

log⁡L≤log⁡2+d​log⁡2+2d​log⁡(N+1).\log L\leq\log 2+d\log 2+2^{d}\log(N+1).

4.3 Finite-index lifting and entropy pruning

We now build the simultaneous shifts into a single lattice. The finite-index hypothesis is the algebraic bridge: after choosing a basis map BB for Λv\Lambda_{v}, the inclusion Ψ⁡(ℤd)⊆Λv\Psi(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} yields a nonsingular integer matrix MM such that Ψ=B∘M\Psi=B\circ M. Since M𝖳M^{\mathsf{T}} is onto on the horizontal torus, the prescribed shifts can be lifted to shear parameters without changing the product of the horizontal and vertical determinants. The next theorem formalizes this construction.

Theorem 4.4.

Let ℝn=E⊕F\mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F be an orthogonal decomposition with dimE=m\dim E=m and dimF=d\dim F=d. Let K⊆E⊕FK\subseteq E\oplus F be compact, and define its horizontal sections by Ky≔{x∈E:x+y∈K}K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\}. Suppose that:

  1. (i)

    J1,…,JN⊆EJ_{1},\ldots,J_{N}\subseteq E are compact sets, and Λh⊆E\Lambda_{h}\subseteq E is a lattice. For each a∈[N]a\in[N], let δa∈[0,1]\delta_{a}\in[0,1] satisfy

    ρ¯​(Λh+Ja)≤δafor every ​a∈[N];\bar{\rho}(\Lambda_{h}+J_{a})\leq\delta_{a}\quad\text{for every }a\in[N];
  2. (ii)

    Λv⊆F\Lambda_{v}\subseteq F is a lattice, Ψ:ℝd→F\Psi\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to F is a linear isomorphism, and Ψ⁡(ℤd)⊆Λv\Psi(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} is a finite-index sublattice;

5 Proof of the universal upper bound

We prove the upper bound in four steps. First, we normalize KK, choose the vertical dimension, and discretize all relevant horizontal sections. Second, the weighted full-cube construction supplies a vertical lattice and a Boolean family of Gaussian loads above every vertical translate. Third, entropy pruning removes the small loads, after which the Rogers–Schmidt estimate gives one horizontal lattice for every surviving section label. Finally, weighted lifting combines the horizontal and vertical lattices, and Rogers’ completion lemma turns the resulting almost covering into an exact covering.

Put ℓn≔log⁡log⁡n\ell_{n}\coloneqq\log\log n. For a sufficiently large absolute constant AA, choose

d≔⌈A​ℓn4/3​(log⁡ℓn)2/3⌉.d\coloneqq\left\lceil A\ell_{n}^{4/3}(\log\ell_{n})^{2/3}\right\rceil. (5.1)

Set m≔n−dm\coloneqq n-d.

For orientation, the Gaussian width is τ=(2​log⁡d)−1\tau=(2\log d)^{-1}, the finite-field grid has size Q≍d​(log⁡d)2Q\asymp d(\log d)^{2}, and the vertical dimension satisfies d≍ℓn4/3​(log⁡ℓn)2/3d\asymp\ell_{n}^{4/3}(\log\ell_{n})^{2/3}. Later, the number of section labels satisfies log⁡N0=O⁡(d​log⁡n)\log N_{0}=O(d\log n), the pruning threshold satisfies T0=O⁡(d​log⁡n)T_{0}=O(d\log n), and the target density is ρ=n​log⁡n​d5/2+o⁡(1)\rho=n\log n\,d^{5/2+o(1)}. The first two parameters define the vertical cube and lattice; the choice of dd provides the required min-entropy; N0N_{0} and T0T_{0} control the common-lattice union bound; and ρ\rho provides the total horizontal load. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, every o⁡(1)o(1) term in this section is deterministic and uniform in the convex body KK, the vertical translate ww, and the Boolean vertex ε\varepsilon.

Part II Worst-case lower bounds

The lower-bound argument is technically independent of Part I. We therefore introduce its spherical, Poisson, and flat-torus notation locally.

6 Tools for the lower bound

The proof uses three auxiliary tools. Spherical-cap estimates control intersections among the sets of Poisson directions that cut prescribed residual vectors. A packing argument on a flat torus produces many targets with separated residual directions. Finally, a continuous Janson inequality converts bounds for the resulting Poisson witnesses and their dependency diagrams into a small covering probability for a fixed lattice.

We write B2nB_{2}^{n} for the Euclidean unit ball, 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1} for its boundary, κn≔voln⁡(B2n)\kappa_{n}\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{n}(B_{2}^{n}), and σ\sigma for the rotation-invariant probability measure on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. Throughout Part II, the symbols cc and CC denote positive absolute constants whose values may change from one occurrence to the next. Every other constant is fixed within the statement or proof in which it is introduced, and the constants in the hierarchy of Section 9 remain fixed thereafter. Any dependence on fixed parameters is stated explicitly.

For r>1r>1, let

pn​(r)≔σ⁡{u∈𝕊n−1:|u1|>1/r}.p_{n}(r)\coloneqq\sigma\{u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\colon|u_{1}|>1/r\}.

For nonzero vectors xx and zz in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, define their projective angle by

∠proj​(x,z)≔min⁡{∠⁡(x,z),π−∠⁡(x,z)}.\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(x,z)\coloneqq\min\{\angle(x,z),\pi-\angle(x,z)\}.

6.1 Spherical caps

The following estimates will be used repeatedly. The uniformity over a shell of width O⁡(log⁡n/n)O(\log n/n) is essential later.

For part (i), apply (6.1) with τ=1/r\tau=1/r. When r=a​et/nr=ae^{t/n}, Taylor expansion gives

For part (ii), put p⁡(ζ)≔∫ζ1fn​(s)​𝑑sp(\zeta)\coloneqq\int_{\zeta}^{1}f_{n}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s. The endpoint estimate implies

−dd​ζ​log⁡p​(ζ)≤C​n-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\zeta}\log p(\zeta)\leq Cn

uniformly on the fixed threshold interval. Integrating from τ\tau to τ+h\tau+h yields

It remains to prove part (iii). Split each absolute cap into two oriented caps. The shell assumptions place all oriented thresholds in a fixed compact interval [τ0,τ1]⊊(0,1)[\tau_{0},\tau_{1}]\subsetneq(0,1) and give

|τ−ξ|≤C2​log⁡nn.|\tau-\xi|\leq C_{2}\frac{\log n}{n}. (6.2)

unless the two constraints have empty intersection with the unit ball.

ℙ[|Pu|2≥q]=(1−q)(n−2)/2for0≤q≤1.\mathbb{P}\left[|Pu|^{2}\geq q\right]=(1-q)^{(n-2)/2}\quad\text{for}\quad 0\leq q\leq 1.

6.2 Unfolding on a flat torus

For a lattice Λ\Lambda, let 𝕋Λ≔ℝn/Λ\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{n}/\Lambda, equipped with normalized Haar measure. If y∈𝕋Λy\in\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, an expression involving the coset y−Λy-\Lambda is evaluated using any representative of yy; the result is independent of that choice. In particular, for every nonnegative measurable function ff, the sum below is a well-defined function on 𝕋Λ\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, and we use the unfolding identity

∫𝕋Λ∑λ∈Λf⁡(y−λ)​𝑑y=1detΛ​∫ℝnf⁡(x)​𝑑x.\int_{\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(y-\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}y=\frac{1}{\det\Lambda}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. (6.6)

To obtain this identity, integrate over a fundamental domain and translate its lattice copies.

The next packing lemma does not require the quotient map to be injective on a small Euclidean ball.

Lemma 6.2.

Let G⊆𝕋ΛG\subseteq\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda} have Haar measure at least γ>0\gamma>0, and let δ>0\delta>0. There are points y1,…,yT∈Gy_{1},\ldots,y_{T}\in G such that dist𝕋Λ⁡(yα−yβ,0)>δ\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}}(y_{\alpha}-y_{\beta},0)>\delta and dist𝕋Λ⁡(yα+yβ,0)>δ\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}}(y_{\alpha}+y_{\beta},0)>\delta for all distinct α\alpha and β\beta, and such that T≥γ​detΛ/(2​κn​δn)T\geq\gamma\det\Lambda/(2\kappa_{n}\delta^{n}).

Proof.

Choose the points greedily. After selecting a point yy, remove from GG the images of the two closed balls y+δ​B2ny+\delta B_{2}^{n} and −y+δ​B2n-y+\delta B_{2}^{n}. The selected points satisfy both separation conditions. Since every δ\delta-separated subset of the compact torus is finite, the process ends with a maximal list y1,…,yTy_{1},\ldots,y_{T}.

The image of a Euclidean ball of radius δ\delta has normalized Haar measure at most κn​δn/detΛ\kappa_{n}\delta^{n}/\det\Lambda; identifications under the quotient map can only decrease its measure. By maximality, the 2​T2T removed images cover GG. Hence

γ≤2​T​κn​δndetΛ,\gamma\leq\frac{2T\kappa_{n}\delta^{n}}{\det\Lambda},

which proves the lemma. ∎

6.3 A continuous Janson inequality

Here a witness is an injective tuple of Poisson points chosen from prescribed measurable slots. The diagram sums below record the ways in which two witnesses can share Poisson points.

Let (Ω,μ)(\Omega,\mu) be a finite nonatomic standard Borel measure space, and let Π\Pi be a Poisson process with intensity measure μ\mu. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a finite index set. For each α∈𝒜\alpha\in\mathcal{A}, let IαI_{\alpha} be a finite nonempty set. For every i∈Iαi\in I_{\alpha}, let Eα​i⊆ΩE_{\alpha i}\subseteq\Omega be measurable with 0<μ⁡(Eα​i)<∞0<\mu(E_{\alpha i})<\infty, and put

λα​i≔μ⁡(Eα​i)andνα≔∏i∈Iαλα​i.\lambda_{\alpha i}\coloneqq\mu(E_{\alpha i})\quad\text{and}\quad\nu_{\alpha}\coloneqq\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\lambda_{\alpha i}.

Let ZαZ_{\alpha} count the injective tuples (ui)i∈Iα(u_{i})_{i\in I_{\alpha}} of points of Π\Pi such that ui∈Eα​iu_{i}\in E_{\alpha i} for every i∈Iαi\in I_{\alpha}. The Campbell–Mecke formula [22] gives

𝔼​Zα=∫Ω≠Iα∏i∈Iα𝟏Eα​i​(ui)​d​μ⊗Iα​((ui)i)=∏i∈Iαλα​i=να,\mathbb{E}Z_{\alpha}=\int_{\Omega_{\neq}^{I_{\alpha}}}\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\mathbf{1}_{E_{\alpha i}}(u_{i})\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{\otimes I_{\alpha}}((u_{i})_{i})=\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\lambda_{\alpha i}=\nu_{\alpha},

where Ω≠Iα\Omega_{\neq}^{I_{\alpha}} is the set of tuples with pairwise distinct coordinates. Its complement has product measure zero because μ\mu is nonatomic. Thus να\nu_{\alpha} is the mean number of witnesses of type α\alpha.

A partial injection M:Iα⇢IβM\colon I_{\alpha}\dashrightarrow I_{\beta} is an injective map from a subset of IαI_{\alpha} into IβI_{\beta}. For a nonempty partial injection MM, define

Wα​β​(M)≔να​νβ​∏(i,j)∈Mμ⁡(Eα​i∩Eβ​j)λα​i​λβ​j.W_{\alpha\beta}(M)\coloneqq\nu_{\alpha}\nu_{\beta}\prod_{(i,j)\in M}\frac{\mu(E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\beta j})}{\lambda_{\alpha i}\lambda_{\beta j}}. (6.7)

We first record the finite indexed form of Janson’s inequality that will be used in the approximation.

Lemma 6.3.

Let (Xv)v∈V(X_{v})_{v\in V} be independent Bernoulli variables on a finite set VV, and let (Hh)h∈ℋ(H_{h})_{h\in\mathcal{H}} be a finite indexed family of nonempty subsets of VV. Repetitions among the underlying subsets are allowed. Put

Δ∗≔∑(h,h′):Hh∩Hh′≠∅𝔼(IhIh′).\Delta^{*}\coloneqq\sum_{(h,h^{\prime})\colon H_{h}\cap H_{h^{\prime}}\neq\varnothing}\mathbb{E}(I_{h}I_{h^{\prime}}).

If m>0m>0, then

ℙ[Y=0]≤exp(−m22​Δ∗).\mathbb{P}\left[Y=0\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{m^{2}}{2\Delta^{*}}\right). (6.8)
Proof.

For distinct underlying subsets, (6.8) is the lower-tail form of Janson’s inequality with t=mt=m; see Janson, Łuczak, and Ruciński [17, Theorem 2.14]. With our ordered convention, Δ∗\Delta^{*} is the quantity denoted there by Δ¯\bar{\Delta}.

To remove the distinctness assumption, fix 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1. For each index hh, introduce a private Bernoulli variable BhB_{h} with parameter 1−ε1-\varepsilon. Their mean and ordered dependency sum are

mε=(1−ε)​mm_{\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon)m

and

Δε∗=(1−ε)​∑h𝔼​Ih+(1−ε)2​∑h≠h′Hh∩Hh′≠∅𝔼⁡(Ih​Ih′).\Delta_{\varepsilon}^{*}=(1-\varepsilon)\sum_{h}\mathbb{E}I_{h}+(1-\varepsilon)^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\neq h^{\prime}\\ H_{h}\cap H_{h^{\prime}}\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}(I_{h}I_{h^{\prime}}).

The probability that the augmented family has no present member differs from ℙ[Y=0]\mathbb{P}\left[Y=0\right] by at most |ℋ|​ε|\mathcal{H}|\varepsilon. Since mε→mm_{\varepsilon}\to m and Δε∗→Δ∗\Delta_{\varepsilon}^{*}\to\Delta^{*}, letting ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 proves the indexed form. ∎

Lemma 6.4.

There is an absolute constant c>0c>0 such that

ℙ[Zα=0 for every α]≤exp(−c(∑ανα)2∑α,βDα​β).\mathbb{P}\left[Z_{\alpha}=0\text{ for every }\alpha\right]\leq\exp\left(-c\frac{(\sum_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha})^{2}}{\sum_{\alpha,\beta}D_{\alpha\beta}}\right). (6.9)

Proof.

We approximate the Poisson process by independent cell-occupancy variables. All sets may first be modified on null sets, so we may assume that they are Borel.

Nested partitions. The standard Borel structure has a countable family of Borel sets that separates points. Start with the Boolean atoms generated by the finitely many sets Eα​iE_{\alpha i}. At stage kk, refine the preceding partition by the first kk point-separating Borel sets. Using nonatomicity, subdivide every positive-measure cell into finitely many measurable pieces of measure at most 2−k2^{-k}. These choices can be made recursively, so they give nested finite partitions (𝒫k)k≥1(\mathcal{P}_{k})_{k\geq 1}. After discarding null cells, we have

δk≔maxC∈𝒫k⁡μ⁡(C)⟶0.\delta_{k}\coloneqq\max_{C\in\mathcal{P}_{k}}\mu(C)\longrightarrow 0.

Every cell is contained in or disjoint from each Eα​iE_{\alpha i}, and every two distinct points of Ω\Omega are eventually separated by the partitions.

For C∈𝒫kC\in\mathcal{P}_{k}, let XCX_{C} indicate that Π\Pi meets CC. The variables (XC)C∈𝒫k(X_{C})_{C\in\mathcal{P}_{k}} are independent, and

qC≔ℙ[XC=1]=1−e−μ⁡(C)=μ(C)(1+O(δk))q_{C}\coloneqq\mathbb{P}\left[X_{C}=1\right]=1-e^{-\mu(C)}=\mu(C)(1+O(\delta_{k})) (6.10)

uniformly in CC.

An indexed hyperedge consists of a label α\alpha and an assignment (Ci)i∈Iα(C_{i})_{i\in I_{\alpha}} of pairwise distinct cells satisfying Ci⊆Eα​iC_{i}\subseteq E_{\alpha i} for every ii. Its underlying vertex set is {Ci:i∈Iα}\{C_{i}\colon i\in I_{\alpha}\}, and its indicator is ∏iXCi\prod_{i}X_{C_{i}}. Different labels and different assignments remain distinct indices even when they have the same underlying cell set. Let YkY_{k} count the present indexed hyperedges, let mk≔𝔼​Ykm_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}Y_{k}, and let Δk∗\Delta_{k}^{*} be the ordered dependency sum from Lemma 6.3. Then

ℙ[Yk=0]≤exp(−mk22​Δk∗)\mathbb{P}\left[Y_{k}=0\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{m_{k}^{2}}{2\Delta_{k}^{*}}\right) (6.11)

whenever mk>0m_{k}>0.

𝔼​Yk,α=(1+O⁡(sα​δk))​∑(Ci)i∈Iα​ pairwise distinctCi⊆Eα​i∏i∈Iαμ⁡(Ci).\mathbb{E}Y_{k,\alpha}=\bigl(1+O(s_{\alpha}\delta_{k})\bigr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(C_{i})_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\text{ pairwise distinct}\\ C_{i}\subseteq E_{\alpha i}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\mu(C_{i}). (6.12)

∑C⊆Eα​i∩Eα​jμ​(C)2​∏ℓ≠i,jλα​ℓ≤δk​μ​(Eα​i∩Eα​j)​∏ℓ≠i,jλα​ℓ.\sum_{C\subseteq E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\alpha j}}\mu(C)^{2}\prod_{\ell\neq i,j}\lambda_{\alpha\ell}\leq\delta_{k}\mu(E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\alpha j})\prod_{\ell\neq i,j}\lambda_{\alpha\ell}.

mk⟶∑ανα.m_{k}\longrightarrow\sum_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}. (6.13)

In particular, mk>0m_{k}>0 for all sufficiently large kk.

Dependency sum. Fix α\alpha, β\beta, and a nonempty partial injection M:Iα⇢IβM\colon I_{\alpha}\dashrightarrow I_{\beta}. Form the quotient of the disjoint union Iα⊔IβI_{\alpha}\sqcup I_{\beta} by identifying ii and jj whenever (i,j)∈M(i,j)\in M. For each quotient class QQ, let FQF_{Q} be the intersection of the one or two slot sets indexed by QQ. The two indexed hyperedges intersect exactly when this partial injection is nonempty. Hence the ordered dependency sum decomposes without omission or repetition over the nonempty partial injections. Limiting event. Because the partitions are nested, the events {Yk>0}\{Y_{k}>0\} increase with kk. 7 The random convex body

The construction has three components. The cube fixes the John normalization, the outer Euclidean ball gives a uniform radius bound, and the random slabs create many potential holes while preserving a constant fraction of the volume with positive probability.

For the remainder of the lower-bound argument, fix

a≔2,L≔a2−1=3,andβ≔1,a\coloneqq 2,\qquad L\coloneqq a^{2}-1=3,\quad\text{and}\quad\beta\coloneqq 1,

This normalization gives M​pn​(a)=LMp_{n}(a)=L, so the cap associated with a residual vector of norm aa has constant intensity. It balances the random cuts against survival of a constant fraction of the volume.

9 Poisson witnesses and the common-lens hierarchy

For a fixed good target, each residual vector in the outer shell determines a cap of Poisson directions that excludes that residual from the random body. We group nearby residual caps into blocks and place a common measurable slot inside every cap in a block. An injective Poisson point in each slot then certifies that the target is uncovered. The hierarchy below controls dependencies among the slots of one target, while the separation from Lemma 8.2 controls dependencies between different targets. We finally apply the continuous Janson inequality to many targets for which the products of the slot measures are comparable.

We make the constant choices as follows. The body and shell parameters aa, AA, and β\beta are fixed first. The geometric estimates in Lemmas 9.2 and 9.3 determine their absolute constants, including A0A_{0}. We then fix ε\varepsilon, take cshc_{\mathrm{sh}} and B0B_{0} from Lemma 9.5, and choose a fixed B≥B0B\geq B_{0}; this determines the anchor exponent CancC_{\mathrm{anc}}. These choices are independent of the tail exponent JJ. After fixing J>0J>0, we choose Dsep=Dsep​(J)D_{\mathrm{sep}}=D_{\mathrm{sep}}(J) sufficiently large for the cross-target estimate and then choose c0=c0​(J)c_{0}=c_{0}(J) sufficiently small. No constant depends on nn, the shape of the lattice, or η\eta.

Fix a good target yy with m⁡(y)≥1m(y)\geq 1, put m≔m⁡(y)m\coloneqq m(y), and list its residuals as

Xyη={x1,…,xm}.X_{y}^{\eta}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\}.

For i∈[m]i\in[m], put

Ci≔Cxiηandci≔μ⁡(Ci)=cη​(xi).C_{i}\coloneqq C_{x_{i}}^{\eta}\quad\text{and}\quad c_{i}\coloneqq\mu(C_{i})=c_{\eta}(x_{i}).

The good-target estimates give

m≤CR,m≤n2,∑i=1mq(ci)≤CR,andn−CA≤ci≤CA.m\leq CR,\qquad m\leq n^{2},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{m}q(c_{i})\leq CR,\quad\text{and}\quad n^{-C_{A}}\leq c_{i}\leq C_{A}. (9.1)

The inequality m≤n2m\leq n^{2} follows from m≤C​Rm\leq CR and R≤c0​n​log⁡nR\leq c_{0}n\log n for sufficiently large nn.

Put

c¯i≔min⁡{ci,1/2}andsi≔−log⁡c¯i.\bar{c}_{i}\coloneqq\min\{c_{i},1/2\}\quad\text{and}\quad s_{i}\coloneqq-\log\bar{c}_{i}.

The truncation keeps the slot scale at most 1/21/2, while sis_{i} records the rarity of the cap. The metric below combines angular energy with mismatch between these logarithmic intensities.

View ei≔xi/|xi|e_{i}\coloneqq x_{i}/|x_{i}| as a point of real projective space. Define

𝔡⁡(i,j)≔n​∠proj​(ei,ej)+|si−sj|.\mathfrak{d}(i,j)\coloneqq\sqrt{n}\,\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j})+\sqrt{|s_{i}-s_{j}|}. (9.2)

The projective angle is the geodesic metric on real projective space. The second summand is also a metric because x+y≤x+y\sqrt{x+y}\leq\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y} for nonnegative xx and yy. Hence 𝔡\mathfrak{d} is a metric, and

n​∠proj​(ei,ej)2+|si−sj|≤𝔡​(i,j)2≤2​n​∠proj​(ei,ej)2+2​|si−sj|.n\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j})^{2}+|s_{i}-s_{j}|\leq\mathfrak{d}(i,j)^{2}\leq 2n\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j})^{2}+2|s_{i}-s_{j}|. (9.3)

For every nonempty set S⊆[m]S\subseteq[m], let

r⁡(S)≔mina∈S⁡maxi∈S​𝔡​(a,i)2.r(S)\coloneqq\min_{a\in S}\max_{i\in S}\mathfrak{d}(a,i)^{2}. (9.4)

The next proposition is the deterministic core of the fixed-target argument. It partitions the residual caps into blocks and assigns a common-lens slot to each block. Later, an injective choice of one Poisson point from every slot will certify that the target is a hole. Estimate (9.5) bounds the negative logarithm of the product of the slot measures, (9.6) controls diagonal identifications, and (9.8) controls off-diagonal identifications after the normalization in (9.7). The last two estimates feed into the self-diagram bound in Lemma 9.6.

All constants are uniform in the lattice, the good target, and 0≤η≤n−40\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.

Pairwise affinity is not enough to assign an entire cluster of caps to one Poisson point. The next lemma gives a quantitative common intersection for caps that are close in the parameter metric.

Terminality prevents too many low-penalty blocks from having anchors near one point. The resulting local-count estimate will be converted into the row-sum bound needed for the self-diagram calculation.

10 Uniformity over all lattices

We now pass from one fixed lattice to all lattices by a finite-net argument. Any lattice covering KΠK_{\Pi} has covering radius at most bb and hence admits a short basis. The determinant range then gives a quantitative lower bound on the least singular value of a basis matrix, allowing us to round it to a finite matrix grid. A hole for the enlarged body is stable under the resulting near-identity linear perturbation. We take J=6J=6 in Proposition 9.7; the resulting probability e−c​n6e^{-cn^{6}} dominates the grid size exp⁡(O⁡(n3​log⁡n))\exp(O(n^{3}\log n)).

For a lattice Λ\Lambda, let covrad⁡(Λ)\operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda) denote its Euclidean covering radius. For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, let λi​(Λ)\lambda_{i}(\Lambda) denote its iith successive minimum with respect to B2nB_{2}^{n}. All unqualified matrix norms in this section are Euclidean operator norms; ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}} denotes the Frobenius norm.

Lemma 10.1.

If covrad⁡(Λ)≤b\operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda)\leq b, then Λ\Lambda has a basis g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n} such that

|gi|≤C​n​bfor1≤i≤n.|g_{i}|\leq Cnb\quad\text{for}\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
Proof.

Jarník’s inequality [18] gives λn​(Λ)≤2​covrad⁡(Λ)\lambda_{n}(\Lambda)\leq 2\operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda); a modern formulation appears in [3, Eq. (12)]. The Mahler basis estimate [12, Eq. (2.5)] gives a basis satisfying

|gi|≤max⁡{1,i/2}​λi​(Λ).|g_{i}|\leq\max\{1,i/2\}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda).

Since λi​(Λ)≤λn​(Λ)\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\leq\lambda_{n}(\Lambda), the desired bound follows. ∎

The enlarged body from (7.2) provides the buffer needed to transfer a hole between nearby lattices.

Lemma 10.2.

Let 0≤η≤n−40\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}. Let GG be an invertible matrix, let Λ≔G​ℤn\Lambda\coloneqq G\mathbb{Z}^{n}, and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be an invertible linear map. Suppose that y∉K^Π,η+Λy\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+\Lambda. If

‖𝒯−I‖≤η4​(b+η),\|\mathcal{T}-I\|\leq\frac{\eta}{4(b+\eta)},

then 𝒯​y∉KΠ+𝒯​Λ\mathcal{T}y\notin K_{\Pi}+\mathcal{T}\Lambda.

Proof.

Fix z∈ℤnz\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, and put x≔y−G​zx\coloneqq y-Gz. Since x∉K^Π,ηx\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}, either |x|>b+η|x|>b+\eta, or some u∈Πu\in\Pi satisfies |⟨u,x⟩|>1+η|\langle u,x\rangle|>1+\eta.

In the first case,

|𝒯​x|≥(1−‖𝒯−I‖)​|x|>(1−‖𝒯−I‖)​(b+η)≥b+3​η4≥b.|\mathcal{T}x|\geq(1-\|\mathcal{T}-I\|)|x|>(1-\|\mathcal{T}-I\|)(b+\eta)\geq b+\frac{3\eta}{4}\geq b.

In the second case, if |x|≤b+η|x|\leq b+\eta, then

|⟨u,𝒯​x⟩|≥|⟨u,x⟩|−‖(𝒯−I)​x‖>1+η−η4=1+3​η4≥1.|\langle u,\mathcal{T}x\rangle|\geq|\langle u,x\rangle|-\|(\mathcal{T}-I)x\|>1+\eta-\frac{\eta}{4}=1+\frac{3\eta}{4}\geq 1.

When |x|>b+η|x|>b+\eta, the first estimate applies. Thus 𝒯​x∉KΠ\mathcal{T}x\notin K_{\Pi} for every z∈ℤnz\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Since 𝒯​x=𝒯​y−𝒯​G​z\mathcal{T}x=\mathcal{T}y-\mathcal{T}Gz, the point 𝒯​y\mathcal{T}y is not covered by KΠ+𝒯​ΛK_{\Pi}+\mathcal{T}\Lambda. ∎

Let cfixc_{\mathrm{fix}} be the upper-range constant supplied by Proposition 9.7 for J=6J=6. Fix cnet>0c_{\mathrm{net}}>0 so small that 2​cnet≤cfix2c_{\mathrm{net}}\leq c_{\mathrm{fix}}, and put

Dn≔κn​ancnet​Fn.D_{n}\coloneqq\frac{\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{c_{\mathrm{net}}F_{n}}. (10.1)
Proposition 10.3.

With probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1), no lattice Λ\Lambda with detΛ≥Dn\det\Lambda\geq D_{n} covers KΠK_{\Pi}.

Proof.

Suppose that KΠ+ΛK_{\Pi}+\Lambda covers. Since KΠ⊆b​B2nK_{\Pi}\subseteq bB_{2}^{n}, the translates of b​B2nbB_{2}^{n} also cover. Hence

covrad⁡(Λ)≤banddetΛ≤κn​bn.\operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda)\leq b\quad\text{and}\quad\det\Lambda\leq\kappa_{n}b^{n}. (10.2)

The determinant bound follows by integrating the covering multiplicity over a fundamental domain.

Now consider a lattice satisfying (10.2) and detΛ≥Dn\det\Lambda\geq D_{n}. By Lemma 10.1, it has a basis matrix G′G^{\prime} whose columns have norm at most C​n​bCnb. Consequently,

‖G′‖≤‖G′‖F≤C​b​n3/2.\|G^{\prime}\|\leq\|G^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\leq Cbn^{3/2}.

Let s1​(G′)≥⋯≥sn​(G′)=smin​(G′)s_{1}(G^{\prime})\geq\cdots\geq s_{n}(G^{\prime})=s_{\min}(G^{\prime}) be the singular values. Since

|detG′|=∏i=1nsi​(G′)≤smin​(G′)​‖G′‖n−1,|\det G^{\prime}|=\prod_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}(G^{\prime})\leq s_{\min}(G^{\prime})\|G^{\prime}\|^{n-1},

we have

smin​(G′)≥Dn(C​b​n3/2)n−1≕s¯n.s_{\min}(G^{\prime})\geq\frac{D_{n}}{(Cbn^{3/2})^{n-1}}\eqqcolon\underline{s}_{n}. (10.3)

Stirling’s formula gives −log⁡κn=(n/2)​log⁡n+O⁡(n)-\log\kappa_{n}=(n/2)\log n+O(n), and hence

−log⁡s¯n=O⁡(n​log⁡n).-\log\underline{s}_{n}=O(n\log n). (10.4)

Set η≔n−5\eta\coloneqq n^{-5}, and define the mesh

ξn≔η​s¯n100​n​(b+η).\xi_{n}\coloneqq\frac{\eta\underline{s}_{n}}{100n(b+\eta)}. (10.5)

Let Γn≔ξn​ℤ∩[−2​C​n​b,2​C​n​b]\Gamma_{n}\coloneqq\xi_{n}\mathbb{Z}\cap[-2Cnb,2Cnb] and let ℬngrid≔Γnn×n\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{grid}}\coloneqq\Gamma_{n}^{n\times n}. Retain the invertible matrices G∈ℬngridG\in\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{grid}} satisfying

Dn2≤|detG|≤2​κn​bn,\frac{D_{n}}{2}\leq|\det G|\leq 2\kappa_{n}b^{n}, (10.6)

and denote this finite set by 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n}.

One entry has at most 1+4​C​n​b/ξn1+4Cnb/\xi_{n} possible values. By (10.4) and η=n−5\eta=n^{-5},

log⁡(1+4​C​n​bξn)=O⁡(n​log⁡n).\log\left(1+\frac{4Cnb}{\xi_{n}}\right)=O(n\log n).

Since there are n2n^{2} entries,

log⁡|𝒢n|=O⁡(n3​log⁡n).\log|\mathcal{G}_{n}|=O(n^{3}\log n). (10.7)

Choose, once and for all, a nearest-point rounding map from [−C​n​b,C​n​b][-Cnb,Cnb] to Γn\Gamma_{n}. Apply it entrywise to G′G^{\prime} and call the rounded matrix GG. The larger interval in the definition of Γn\Gamma_{n} ensures that the rounded entries remain in the grid box. Also,

‖G−G′‖≤‖G−G′‖F≤n​ξn.\|G-G^{\prime}\|\leq\|G-G^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\leq n\xi_{n}. (10.8)

By Weyl’s inequality and (10.3),

smin​(G)≥s¯n−n​ξn≥12​s¯ns_{\min}(G)\geq\underline{s}_{n}-n\xi_{n}\geq\frac{1}{2}\underline{s}_{n}

for sufficiently large nn. In particular, GG is invertible.

Put

E≔(G−G′)​(G′)−1.E\coloneqq(G-G^{\prime})(G^{\prime})^{-1}.

Equation (10.8) gives

‖E‖≤n​ξns¯n=η100​(b+η)<12.\|E\|\leq\frac{n\xi_{n}}{\underline{s}_{n}}=\frac{\eta}{100(b+\eta)}<\frac{1}{2}. (10.9)

Since G=(I+E)​G′G=(I+E)G^{\prime}, every singular value of I+EI+E lies in [1−‖E‖,1+‖E‖][1-\|E\|,1+\|E\|]. Therefore

|log⁡|detG||detG′||=|log⁡|det(I+E)||≤2​n|E|=O⁡(n−4).\left|\log\frac{|\det G|}{|\det G^{\prime}|}\right|=|\log|\det(I+E)||\leq 2n\|E\|=O(n^{-4}). (10.10)

The inequalities Dn≤|detG′|≤κn​bnD_{n}\leq|\det G^{\prime}|\leq\kappa_{n}b^{n} now imply (10.6) for sufficiently large nn. Thus G∈𝒢nG\in\mathcal{G}_{n}.

The linear map from the grid lattice to the original lattice is

𝒯≔G′​G−1=(I+E)−1.\mathcal{T}\coloneqq G^{\prime}G^{-1}=(I+E)^{-1}.

By (10.9),

‖𝒯−I‖≤‖E‖1−‖E‖≤2​‖E‖≤η4​(b+η).\|\mathcal{T}-I\|\leq\frac{\|E\|}{1-\|E\|}\leq 2\|E\|\leq\frac{\eta}{4(b+\eta)}. (10.11)

For every retained grid lattice G​ℤnG\mathbb{Z}^{n}, its parameter RR satisfies

e−β2=an2​bn≤R≤2​κn​anDn=2​cnet​Fn≤cfix​Fn.\frac{e^{-\beta}}{2}=\frac{a^{n}}{2b^{n}}\leq R\leq\frac{2\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{D_{n}}=2c_{\mathrm{net}}F_{n}\leq c_{\mathrm{fix}}F_{n}.

In particular, R≥c∗R\geq c_{*}, so Proposition 9.7 applies uniformly with η=n−5\eta=n^{-5}. By (10.7) and a union bound,

ℙ[K^Π,η+Gℤn covers for some G∈𝒢n]≤exp(O(n3logn)−cn6)=o(1).\mathbb{P}\left[\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+G\mathbb{Z}^{n}\text{ covers for some }G\in\mathcal{G}_{n}\right]\leq\exp\bigl(O(n^{3}\log n)-cn^{6}\bigr)=o(1). (10.12)

On the complementary event, every retained grid lattice has a hole for K^Π,η\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}. Suppose to the contrary that an actual lattice Λ≔G′​ℤn\Lambda\coloneqq G^{\prime}\mathbb{Z}^{n} with detΛ≥Dn\det\Lambda\geq D_{n} covers KΠK_{\Pi}. The preceding rounding argument supplies a matrix G∈𝒢nG\in\mathcal{G}_{n}. Choose y∉K^Π,η+G​ℤny\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+G\mathbb{Z}^{n}. By (10.11) and Lemma 10.2,

𝒯​y∉KΠ+𝒯​G​ℤn=KΠ+G′​ℤn,\mathcal{T}y\notin K_{\Pi}+\mathcal{T}G\mathbb{Z}^{n}=K_{\Pi}+G^{\prime}\mathbb{Z}^{n},

contrary to the assumed covering. This contradiction proves the proposition. ∎

11 Proofs of the main results

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let VV be the event voln⁡(KΠ)≥cv​κn​an\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{\Pi})\geq c_{v}\kappa_{n}a^{n}. By Proposition 7.1, ℙ⁡[V]≥cp>0\mathbb{P}\left[V\right]\geq c_{p}>0. Let UU be the event that no lattice of determinant at least DnD_{n} covers KΠK_{\Pi}. By Proposition 10.3, ℙ⁡[U]=1−o⁡(1)\mathbb{P}\left[U\right]=1-o(1). Therefore

ℙ⁡[U∩V]≥ℙ⁡[V]−ℙ⁡[Uc]≥cp−o⁡(1)>0\mathbb{P}\left[U\cap V\right]\geq\mathbb{P}\left[V\right]-\mathbb{P}\left[U^{\mathrm{c}}\right]\geq c_{p}-o(1)>0

for sufficiently large nn. Fix a realization in U∩VU\cap V, and denote the resulting body by KnK_{n}.

Every lattice Λ\Lambda that covers KnK_{n} satisfies detΛ<Dn\det\Lambda<D_{n}. Hence

voln⁡(Kn)detΛ≥cv​κn​anDn=cv​cnet​n​log⁡n.\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{n})}{\det\Lambda}\geq\frac{c_{v}\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{D_{n}}=c_{v}c_{\mathrm{net}}n\log n.

Since KnK_{n} is origin-symmetric by construction, taking the infimum over all covering lattices proves Theorem 1.3 with c=cv​cnetc=c_{v}c_{\mathrm{net}}. By Proposition 7.1, the John ellipsoid of KnK_{n} is B2nB_{2}^{n}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The lower inequality follows from Theorem 1.3. Every origin-symmetric convex body is a convex body, so the definitions give ΘLsym​(n)≤ΘLconv​(n)\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n). The upper inequality follows from Theorem 1.2. Taking cc from Theorem 1.3 and CC and εn\varepsilon_{n} from Theorem 1.2 proves Theorem 1.1. ∎
